title: Continuous-space occupancy models

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a new class of spatial occupancy models using a clipped Gaussian process to infer species distributions in continuous space.

abstract: Occupancy models are commonly used to infer species distributions over large spatial extents while accounting for imperfect detection. Current approaches, however, are unable to model species occurrence over continuous spatial domains while accounting for the discrete spatial domain of the observed data. We develop a new class of spatial occupancy models that embeds a change of spatial support between the observed data and occurrence process. We use a clipped Gaussian process to represent species occurrence in continuous space which can provide inferences at a finer resolution than the observed occupancy data. Our approach is beneficial because it allows for more realistic models of species occurrence, can account for species occurring in only a portion of a surveyed site, and can relate detection probabilities to these within-site occurrence proportions. We show how our model can be fit using Bayesian methods and develop a computationally efficient MCMC algorithm. We also show how our framework can be extended to handle multiple years of data to learn about species occupancy dynamics in continuous space. We demonstrate our model using simulated data and compare our approach to alternative spatial occupancy models. We also use our model to analyze ovenbird occurrence data collected in New Hampshire, USA.
speaker: Wilson Wright

title: Understanding CNN Efficiency: Statistical Generative Models for Unstructured Image Data

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces novel statistical generative models to analyze the efficiency and approximation capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks in image analysis.

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are foundational in modern image analysis due to their ability to efficiently learn feature representations. However, theoretical understanding of their efficiency remains limited, largely due to inadequate modeling of image structures and their interaction with CNNs. To address this, we introduce novel statistical generative models (SGMs) that decompose images into task-relevant signals and noise, capturing the complexities of natural image data. Based on these SGMs, we propose a feature mapping approach (FMA) to characterize the transformation from raw image data to feature vectors. We analyze CNNs' approximation capabilities, their adaptation to low-dimensional structures, and their efficiency in vision tasks, ultimately developing statistical learning theories for CNN-based image analysis. Our findings reveal the challenges inherent in vision tasks and highlight CNNs' remarkable efficiency in addressing them, providing new insights into their theoretical and practical capabilities. This is based on the joint work with Dr. Guohao Shen.

title: ML/AI-accelerated autonomous experimentation with digital twins: a statistician's playground

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores how machine learning and AI can accelerate autonomous scientific experimentation using digital twin simulators.

abstract: An emerging use of ML/AI in science is autonomous scientific experimentation, which has shown promise for self-driving laboratories in, e.g., material and biotech engineering. This automation is fueled by the rise of "digital twin" simulators that enable reliable virtual experimentation of complex physical systems. One bottleneck, however, is the time-intensive nature of virtual experiments, which can take thousands of CPU hours to perform on a supercomputer. In this talk, we explore several ways that ML/AI can accelerate autonomous experimentation for timely scientific decision-making. The first is the use of physics-informed ML/AI models that incorporate known physics, e.g., boundary information, to enhance model learning from experimental data. The second is the use of ML/AI-enhanced optimization solvers to effectively design experimental runs for complex high-dimensional systems. Time permitting, the third is the use of robust transfer learning models that effectively transfer information from existing literature (e.g., extracted via large language models) to guide experimentation. We explore the effectiveness of these approaches in ongoing scientific collaborations.
speaker: Simon Mak

title: Statistical Foundations of Deep Learning: Toward Efficient and Trustworthy AI

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a statistical perspective on deep learning, highlighting Bayesian neural networks and theoretical validation for trustworthy AI.

abstract: Deep learning has transformed modern artificial intelligence through increasingly flexible models, large datasets, and scalable computation. For statisticians, however, its rapid development raises fundamental questions about statistical modeling, inference, theory, and computational efficiency. In this talk, we present a statistical perspective on deep learning, focusing on Bayesian neural networks, variational inference, theoretical validation, and structurally sparse deep networks. We discuss how statistical modeling and optimization can provide theoretical guarantees, quantify approximation effects, and produce more efficient deep-learning models without substantial loss of predictive performance. Applications to high-dimensional and complex data illustrate the role of statistical methodology in developing reliable and computationally efficient AI. More broadly, the talk explores how statistical theory, machine learning, and optimization can work together to build more principled and trustworthy AI.

title: Early-stopped aggregation: Adaptive inference with computational efficiency

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces early-stopped aggregation, a novel framework for efficient model aggregation in Bayesian and frequentist settings.

abstract: When considering a model selection or, more generally, an aggregation approach for adaptive statistical inference, it is often necessary to compute estimators over a wide range of model complexities including unnecessarily large models even when the true data-generating process is relatively simple, due to the lack of prior knowledge. This requirement can lead to substantial computational inefficiency. In this work, we propose a novel framework for efficient model aggregation called the early-stopped aggregation (ESA): instead of computing and aggregating estimators for all candidate models, we compute only a small number of simpler ones using an early-stopping criterion and aggregate only these for final inference. Our framework is versatile and applies to both Bayesian model selection, in particular, within the variational Bayes framework, and frequentist estimation, including a general penalized estimation setting. We investigate adaptive optimal property of the ESA approach across three learning paradigms. We first show that ESA achieves optimal adaptive contraction rates in the variational Bayes setting under mild conditions. We extend this result to variational empirical Bayes, where prior hyperparameters are chosen in a data-dependent manner. In addition, we apply the ESA approach to frequentist aggregation including both penalization-based and sample-splitting implementations, and establish corresponding theory. As we demonstrate, there is a clear unification between early-stopped Bayes and frequentist penalized aggregation, with a common "energy" functional comprising a data-fitting term and a complexity-control term that drives both procedures. We further present several applications and numerical studies that highlight the efficiency and strong performance of the proposed approach.

title: From Managing Teams to Managing Agents

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses the transition from managing human teams to managing agent systems.

abstract: Over the past 20 years, my job has evolved from writing code, to building and leading engineering teams, and now, somewhat unexpectedly, back toward building software, this time alongside AI agents. In this talk, I’ll share what it looks like to work on a small, AI-forward engineering team where agents are becoming part of the everyday development process. We’ll look at what AI is genuinely good at today, where it still falls short, and how the role of a software engineer changes when writing code is no longer the only, or even the primary, way you contribute to a codebase. Drawing on my experience as an engineer, engineering executive, and now a leader of a small team building heavily with AI, I’ll explore the surprising similarities between managing people and managing agents: providing context, breaking down problems, delegating work, reviewing results, and knowing when to step in. Most importantly, we’ll talk about what these changes might mean for students entering the workforce now, and which skills become more valuable, not less, as AI becomes a bigger part of how we build software.

title: C is for Communications and the Cosmos

annotations.one_line_context: A NASA leader reflects on a four-decade career spanning satellite communications, RF, and laser technology for deep space missions.

abstract: In the early 1980s, an average, self-described shy electrical engineering student sat in a Virginia Tech classroom, discovering satellite communications for the first time. Over the next four decades, those foundational lessons became the launchpad for an extraordinary career at NASA. This talk tracks that journey from Blacksburg to the stars, exploring how a technical foundation in RF and emerging laser communications helped reshape how NASA transmits mission data. Discover how technical expertise evolved into leadership, ultimately guiding NASA’s most prestigious flagship astrophysics missions to unlock the secrets of the cosmos.

title: Startups: The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly

annotations.one_line_context: A seasoned executive and venture partner offers engineering students a practical framework for navigating the startup founder journey.

abstract: Most engineers who want to build a company will make the same mistakes – not because they lack technical skills, but because no one gave them an honest picture of what founding a company actually involves. This session draws on thirty years of experience as an operator, executive, and venture capital partner – across multiple industries, company builds, exits, and investment decisions – to give engineering students a practical framework for the founder journey. Topics include the mistakes founders most commonly make, what venture capitalists are actually looking for and how founders tend to misread that relationship, and what a realistic path from engineer to founder looks like. The lessons are drawn from specific experiences – some successful, some not.

title: From Virginia Tech to Silicon Valley: Navigating the AI Revolution — Career Insights, Tech Trends and Opportunities.

annotations.one_line_context: A Meta product management director discusses AI trends, industry transformations, and career guidance for emerging professionals.

abstract: The technology industry is undergoing a seismic transformation driven by artificial intelligence. In this talk, Wattoo—a Virginia Tech alumnus and Director of Product Management at Meta—shares his 20+ year career journey from the halls of Virginia Tech to leadership roles at Qualcomm, Amazon, and Meta, spanning semiconductors, smartphones, cloud infrastructure, and AI. Wattoo will explore the key industry trends shaping AI today—from foundation models and generative AI to the infrastructure powering them at scale—and what these shifts mean for the broader tech landscape. He will then turn his focus to what matters most for students and emerging professionals: how to position yourself for success in this rapidly evolving field, what skills and mindsets are most valuable, and how to identify and seize the opportunities that AI is creating across every sector. Whether you're studying engineering, computer science, business, or any discipline intersecting with technology, this talk will equip you with a practitioner's perspective on where the industry is headed and how you can be part of shaping it.

title: You Don't Have to Be the Smartest Engineer in the Room

annotations.one_line_context: A tech CTO shares how understanding business drivers, customer needs, and team mechanics can make an engineer uniquely valuable.

abstract: I got my first job at a haptics startup a decade before haptics was a thing. Everybody seemed smarter than me, so I had to find another way to be valuable. I got curious about everything that wasn't my job. What customers were trying to do. How the company made money. Why the plan kept changing. Twenty-six years and four companies later, I've run engineering on three continents for a public company and co-founded one I helped grow from 5 to 500. This talk is about the levers — what drives your team, your boss, your business — and how they shift under venture, private-equity, or public ownership. Understanding them made me more valuable than my technical work ever could. I'll help you see them, too.

title: An Unscheduled Landing in Aerospace

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores the engineering rigor behind safety-critical flight and engine control systems through the career journey of an aerospace engineer.

abstract: When graduating with an engineering degree, few careers follow a straight line. Fewer still are planned down to the exact subfield destination. In this talk, John Daniel shares his journey from writing and testing low-level C and assembly code running on DSPs for tactical radios to directing multidisciplinary teams developing safety-critical flight and engine control systems. Drawing from experience across the entire product lifecycle, Daniel will discuss the engineering rigor behind systems that can never be safe enough, the power of embracing high-stakes opportunities, and how curiosity outside your job description can define your career.
speaker: John Daniel

title: My Journey to Make AI More Approachable

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses resource-aware system designs like ZeRO-Offload and BloomBee that make large-scale AI training and inference more accessible without massive GPU clusters.

abstract: Today’s most capable AI models often require massive GPU clusters and infrastructure available to only a small number of organizations. Li's research asks a different question: Can we redesign AI systems so that more people can use the computing resources already available to them? In this talk, Li will share two steps in his journey to make AI more approachable. ZeRO-Offload combines CPU and GPU resources to enable efficient training of models with more than 13 billion parameters on a single consumer-class GPU. BloomBee extends this vision to inference by coordinating heterogeneous, geographically distributed devices over bandwidth-constrained internet connections. Together, these projects demonstrate how resource-aware system design can lower the barriers to large-scale AI and move AI computation beyond expensive, centralized GPU clusters.

title: Hype to Value: Finding Durable Signal in AI Noise

annotations.one_line_context: This talk examines how companies cut through AI hype to make high-stakes decisions and integrate artificial intelligence into their products and workflows.

abstract: Every company claims to have an AI strategy — but what does that actually mean in practice? Behind the announcements, organizations are making high-stakes decisions with incomplete information, caught between competitive pressures and employees whose work is being rapidly reshaped. Drawing on firsthand experience, this talk will look at how companies are trying to answer the questions they're all wrestling with: How does AI change the way we work? How do we incorporate AI into the products and services we offer? And how will it reshape our customers' relationships with us?
speaker: Andrew Hall

title: Grog Finds a Rock: What Cavemen, Cost, and Coordination Teach Us About AI

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores the practical application, coordination, and cost considerations of adopting artificial intelligence in engineering workflows.

abstract: Meet Grog, a fictional fellow who finds a powerful new tool—a rock—and immediately tries to use it for everything. His learning curve mirrors a challenge facing nearly every company adopting AI: capability does not guarantee fit. Tracy Gregorio, CEO of G2 Ops, shares how G2 Ops moved from early AI experimentation to practical applications in engineering workflows and internal operations. Following Grog from one rock to a coordinated crew, she will discuss what G2 Ops learned about coordinating AI, verifying its work, protecting data, and matching the tool—and its cost—to the job. The discussion will also examine how AI is reshaping engineering work, placing greater emphasis on defining objectives, designing workflows, and verifying results. Blending hard-won experience with humor, this talk is about how companies are wrestling with AI—and what it means for the students about to enter that fight.
speaker: Tracy Gregorio

title: Building Real-World AI Evals for Complex Systems

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses dynamic, human-in-the-loop evaluation frameworks needed to measure large language models and agentic workflows in real-world use.

abstract: Large language models and agentic workflows are advancing faster than our ability to measure them. Traditional engineering benchmarks do not consistently capture how these systems behave in the hands of real users. Drawing on experience across healthcare, consumer tech, and design, this talk makes the case for what the next generation of engineers will need to build instead: dynamic, human-in-the-loop evaluation frameworks that sit at the intersection of core systems engineering and human-computer interaction.
speaker: Setor Zilevu

title: Explicit computations in number theory

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores the interplay between theory and computation in number theory, demonstrating how hidden structures in polynomial equations and curves lead to practical and verifiable algorithms.

abstract: In this talk, we will explore the flow of ideas between theory and computation in number theory. Through examples involving polynomial equations and curves, we will see how apparently random behavior reveals hidden structure. We will explain how this perspective leads to practical algorithms, and how to certify that their answers are correct.
